issues.legal_issue: A decree passed by a court with jurisdiction is not a nullity merely because of an alleged defect in notice or procedure, and its validity cannot be challenged collaterally in execution unless the court lacked inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: A landlord brought a possession suit against the deceased tenant’s heirs for arrears of rent.
The landlord tried to identify and notify the heirs, sent notices by post, and affixed a notice at the premises after other service attempts did not provide the heirs’ details.
An advocate appeared for the defendants, partly cross-examined the landlord’s witness, and later withdrew after stating that he had no instructions.
The trial court had jurisdiction over the subject matter and entered a possession decree; the decree was challenged in execution as void because of alleged defects in notice and the parties named.
issues.conclusion: The decree was not void or inexecutable. Any challenge to alleged errors or procedural irregularities had to be pursued in appropriate proceedings to set it aside, rather than by a collateral challenge in execution.
issues.legal_principle: A decree is a nullity when the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction; a mere error, wrong exercise of jurisdiction, or procedural irregularity does not make it void. An executing court ordinarily cannot go behind the decree, and a jurisdictional defect must be patent for the executing court to treat the decree as a nullity. The Court relied on Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, Seth Hiralal Patni v. Sri Kali Nath, Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v. Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, Rafique Bibi v. Sayed Waliuddin, Malkarjun Bin Shidramappa Pasare v. Narhari Bin Shivappa, Ittavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey, and Bhawarlal v. Universal Heavy Mechanical Lifting Enterprises.

predicates.execution_or_collateral_challenge: A person challenges the decree in execution or in another proceeding collateral to the proceeding in which it was entered.
predicates.decree_passed_by_competent_court: The court that entered the decree had jurisdiction over the subject matter of the case.
predicates.alleged_defect_is_nonjurisdictional: The challenge concerns an error or procedural defect rather than a patent lack of the court’s inherent jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a decree is challenged collaterally, it remains binding until set aside if the court had jurisdiction and the alleged defect was nonjurisdictional.

issues.legal_issue: A subtenant who claims through a tenant is not a necessary party to a landlord’s possession suit against the tenant, and omission of the subtenant does not prevent the decree from binding the subtenant.
material_facts: The possession suit was brought by the landlord against the deceased tenant’s heirs, not against the obstructionists.
The obstructionists claimed through the deceased tenant and were, at most, subtenants; they did not claim to be tenants directly of the landlord.
The obstructionists were not joined as defendants in the possession suit.
The landlord obtained a possession decree against the tenant’s heirs after the tenancy had been terminated.
issues.conclusion: The obstructionists were not necessary parties to the suit. Their non-joinder did not make the decree void or inexecutable, and the decree bound them as persons claiming through the tenant.
issues.legal_principle: A necessary party is one without whom no effective order can be made; a proper party is one whose presence may be needed for a complete decision even though an effective order can be made without them. In a landlord’s possession suit against a tenant, a subtenant is not a necessary party, and a decree based on a valid termination of the tenant’s tenancy binds the subtenant even if the subtenant is not joined. The Court relied on Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member, Board of Revenue, Bihar, M/s. Importers and Manufacturers Ltd. v. Pheroze Framroze Taraporewala, and Rupchand Gupta v. Raghvanshi (Pvt.) Ltd.

rule.if: landlord_possession_suit_against_tenant and tenant_tenancy_terminated and claimant_claims_through_tenant and claimant_not_joined_in_suit

predicates.landlord_possession_suit_against_tenant: A landlord brings a suit for possession against a tenant.
predicates.tenant_tenancy_terminated: The landlord terminates the tenant’s tenancy before bringing the possession suit.
predicates.claimant_claims_through_tenant: The person asserting an interest in the premises claims through the tenant rather than as a direct tenant of the landlord.
predicates.claimant_not_joined_in_suit: The person claiming through the tenant is not made a party to the possession suit.

issues.definition: A possession decree against a tenant binds a person claiming through that tenant even when that person was not joined in the suit.
